opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it goes back to how we framed things in the nested learning work. A model isn't one monolithic thing with "parameters" on one side and "context" on the other. It's a collection of memory systems, each compressing its own stream of information and each updating at a different frequency. Attention is a very fast, very high-fidelity memory with a short horizon. The MLP blocks are much slower and store knowledge that's been compressed over pretraining. In between, you can have a continuum of memories at different timescales.

Why does distillation between them matter for abstraction? When information moves from a fast memory to a slower one, it can't move over verbatim. The slower memory has less capacity relative to everything it's seen, and it updates less often, so it's forced to keep only what generalizes across many contexts. That's essentially the definition of abstraction: the particulars get dropped and the structure survives. So distillation isn't just copying knowledge somewhere more permanent. The compression itself is what produces the more abstract representation.

There's a nice parallel with the neuroscience of memory consolidation. The hippocampus encodes episodes quickly, and then during sleep and replay that information is gradually consolidated into the cortex. What ends up in cortex isn't the episode. It's more like schemas, the regularities across many episodes. I'm careful not to push brain analogies too far, but that multi-timescale consolidation is a big part of why humans can keep learning for a lifetime without overwriting everything, and why the knowledge becomes more general over time.

Compare that with current LLMs. They mostly have two extremes: in-context memory that disappears when the context window ends, and frozen weights that only change during training. There's no pathway for what the model figures out in context to gradually move into more persistent, more abstract knowledge. That's a kind of anterograde amnesia. The model can't form new long-term memories after deployment. If you just fine-tune on new data directly, you get catastrophic forgetting, because you're writing specifics into a memory that's supposed to hold general knowledge.

So with a hierarchy of memories where each level distills into the next, you get two things at once. First, continual learning becomes more stable: the fast levels absorb new, noisy, specific information, and only what's consistently useful propagates to the slow levels. Second, the slow levels naturally become more abstract, because they're effectively learning across the learning of the faster levels. You can think of it as meta-learning emerging from the structure: the higher-level memory learns how to learn, or learns the invariants, rather than the instances.

I'd also say the hard open questions sit there. What's the right objective for the transfer? How often should each level update? How do you decide what's worth consolidating versus forgetting? Those are design choices we're still exploring. But conceptually, I think this layered distillation is one of the most promising routes to models that keep getting smarter from experience, not just bigger from pretraining.

r001.rationale: The response says slower memories have less capacity and receive distilled information, but does not say activating new parameters at the next level frees capacity for new knowledge.

r002.rationale: It describes dropping particulars across episodes or contexts while retaining shared structure as schemas or a more abstract representation.

r003.rationale: It characterizes fast memories as high-fidelity and short-horizon, storing new, noisy, specific information, while slower memories retain general structure.

r004.rationale: It explains that a slower memory has less capacity relative to what it has seen, so compression forces it to retain what generalizes rather than particulars.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that memory in these systems shouldn't be one thing. In our work on nested learning and the Hope-style architectures, you have multiple memory components that update at different frequencies. Some are fast — they're updating every few tokens, basically keeping track of what's happening right now in the context. Others are slow — they update rarely, maybe once per long chunk, or they're closer to what we'd normally call the "weights" of the model.

Now, the question is: how does information move from the fast components to the slow ones? If you just let the slow memory see the raw data stream directly, it's going to be bombarded with noise. Most of the tokens coming in are details — specific names, specific numbers, the exact phrasing of some sentence. That's not what you want a slow, long-term memory to store. You want it to store the things that are stable, that keep showing up, that generalize across many contexts.

And that's really what distillation does. When the fast memory has already compressed a window of experience into its own state, and then the slower memory learns from the fast memory rather than from the raw tokens, it's learning from something that's already been filtered. The fast component has already thrown away a lot of the surface detail, because it had to — it has limited capacity and it's being overwritten constantly. So what survives in it is a kind of summary. And the slow memory distilling from that summary is, in effect, extracting the regularities of the regularities.

If you stack this across several levels, each level is further removed from the raw stream and closer to what I'd call abstract structure. The fastest level knows "this specific user said X three sentences ago." A middle level knows something like "in this document, the discussion is about this topic and it has this structure." The slowest level knows "when documents look like this, this kind of reasoning tends to work." That hierarchy of abstraction isn't something we design by hand. It emerges from the fact that each component is trained to predict or match a component that's already compressed.

There's also a nice connection to how we think the brain does this — the idea that the hippocampus stores episodes quickly and then, over time, the cortex consolidates them into more general knowledge. Memory consolidation during sleep is basically a distillation process. The fast store replays, the slow store learns from the replay, and the slow store ends up with the gist rather than the episodes.

And from a continual learning standpoint, this matters a lot because the main failure mode is catastrophic forgetting — you learn something new and you overwrite something old. If your slow memory is only ever being updated with abstract, distilled signal, it's much less likely to be destabilized by any one specific input. The fast memory absorbs the shock, so to speak. So distillation between the levels gives you both: the ability to adapt quickly to what's in front of you, and a slowly growing, increasingly abstract understanding that doesn't get wiped out every time something new comes in.

r001.rationale: It describes fast and slow memories, but does not say that activating parameters at the next level frees capacity for new knowledge.

r002.rationale: It says compressed memories retain summaries and regularities, but does not describe replacing memorized examples with one generalized representation of their shared concept.

r003.rationale: It characterizes fast memory as tracking recent, specific details and contrasts it with slower memory that captures abstract structure and general patterns.

r004.rationale: It connects limited capacity and distillation with extracting regularities, but does not explain that distilling into fewer parameters forces the learner to capture underlying patterns.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that different memory components operate at different timescales. A fast memory can capture the details of what you’re experiencing right now, while a slower memory accumulates information across many experiences. Distillation is a way to transfer what the fast memory has learned into that slower memory.

But the important part is that you’re not simply copying everything. If you copied every detail, you would just have another store of individual experiences. Instead, the transfer has to favor structure that is useful across experiences. What keeps recurring? What helps you make predictions in different contexts? That creates an opportunity to retain the common pattern while becoming less dependent on the specifics of any one example.

And that’s the connection to abstraction. You move from remembering particular cases toward learning something that explains multiple cases. For a continual learner, this can happen repeatedly as new experience arrives, rather than only during a separate training phase. I wouldn’t say distillation automatically produces abstract understanding, but it gives us a mechanism through which that understanding could develop.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transferring knowledge from fast to slower memory, but does not say that activating new parameters frees capacity for new knowledge.

r002.rationale: It describes retaining common patterns and relying less on specific examples, but does not clearly say that memorized examples are replaced by a single generalized representation.

r003.rationale: It says fast memory captures current details, while abstraction comes from retaining patterns across experiences, connecting fast memory with details rather than conceptual understanding.

r004.rationale: It says transfer should favor recurring structure, but does not explain that distilling knowledge into fewer parameters forces the learner to capture general patterns.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that different memory components operate at different timescales. A fast memory can capture the details of a particular experience, while a slower memory accumulates information across many experiences. Distillation gives us a way to transfer what the fast memory has learned into that slower component.

But the important thing is that this transfer shouldn’t simply copy every experience. If the slower component has limited capacity and is updated across many different situations, it has to capture structure that is useful across those situations. The details might change, but some relationships keep appearing. Those relationships are what we would like it to consolidate.

For example, you might encounter several problems that look very different on the surface but require the same underlying operation. A fast memory can learn each particular solution. Through consolidation, the slower memory can potentially learn the shared operation, so the next problem becomes easier to learn.

So abstraction, from this perspective, is partly a consequence of learning across timescales. You preserve the ability to adapt to a new experience, while gradually building knowledge that generalizes beyond that experience. Distillation doesn’t guarantee that the right abstraction emerges—the objectives and the architecture matter—but it provides a mechanism for that to happen within a continual learner.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention activating new parameters at the next memory level or freeing capacity for new knowledge.

r002.rationale: It contrasts learning particular solutions in fast memory with consolidating their shared operation in slower memory, describing a generalized representation in place of individual examples.

r003.rationale: It says fast memory captures details and particular solutions, while slower memory consolidates shared structure, connecting fast memory to example-level learning rather than conceptual understanding.

r004.rationale: Although it says limited capacity encourages capturing shared structure, it does not explain that distilling knowledge into fewer parameters forces the learner to find general patterns.
